SIRUP (Spatial Immune Receptor Utilities Package) is an R package for spatial adaptive immune receptor repertoire sequencing (spAIRR-seq). It works with B cell receptor (BCR) and T cell receptor (TCR) sequences that carry a spatial barcode, together with spatial gene expression from the same tissue section.

SIRUP covers three stages:

  1. Process. Turn demultiplexed long reads into consensus receptor sequences in an AIRR table, with one spatial ID per sequence. See vignette("processing", package = "SIRUP").
  2. Integrate. Put the receptor table and the spatial Seurat object into one SIRUP object. This vignette starts here.
  3. Analyze and visualize. Draw tissue regions, measure clonal dominance and diversity, test spatial association, and plot lineage trees on the tissue.

This vignette takes about 15 minutes. It shows the SIRUP object, the main plots, and a first regional analysis. The other vignettes go deeper:

Vignette Topic
vignette("processing", package = "SIRUP") Reads to AIRR tables with IgBLAST and pRESTO
vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP") Tissue regions, clonal dominance, and diversity
vignette("spatial-statistics", package = "SIRUP") Moran’s I, Lee’s L, Ripley’s cross K, join counts
vignette("clones-and-trees", package = "SIRUP") Clones, germlines, and lineage trees on the tissue
vignette("multisample", package = "SIRUP") Several sections, bulk AIRR-seq, and blood

Installation

Install SIRUP from GitHub:

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("hoehnlab/SIRUP")

SIRUP uses Seurat objects for spatial expression. Most analysis functions also use packages from the Immcantation framework and from the spatial statistics community. Install the packages that the vignettes use:

install.packages(c(
  "Seurat", "airr", "alakazam", "scoper", "dowser", "spdep", "spatstat.explore",
  "spatstat.geom", "spatstat.random", "cowplot", "patchwork", "pals"
))
BiocManager::install("ggtree")

The processing step also needs command-line tools: IgBLAST, pRESTO, vsearch, and MUSCLE. The airrblast R package, which SIRUP installs, runs IgBLAST. You need them only to process raw reads. The processing vignette tells you how to set them up.

The example data

SIRUP includes a small spAIRR-seq data set from the thymus of a patient with myasthenia gravis (MG). The thymus in MG can contain ectopic germinal centers (eGCs): germinal centers that form outside the lymph nodes and tonsils. The data come from two 10x Visium sections of the same thymus. Each 55 µm spot can hold several cells.

The files are in the package extdata folder:

extdata <- system.file("extdata", package = "SIRUP")
list.files(extdata)
#>  [1] "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz" 
#>  [2] "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz" 
#>  [3] "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz"
#>  [4] "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz"
#>  [5] "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz"       
#>  [6] "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz"       
#>  [7] "mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz"          
#>  [8] "mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz"          
#>  [9] "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv"     
#> [10] "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial.rds"         
#> [11] "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz"          
#> [12] "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"     
#> [13] "mg_thymus_slice2_reads.tsv.gz"        
#> [14] "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"         
#> [15] "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz"
File Contents
mg_thymus_slice*_spatial.rds Seurat object for each section: every spot, a panel of genes, and a lowres H&E image
mg_thymus_slice*_bcr.tsv.gz IGH consensus sequences of each section, as processSpatialSample() wrote them
mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz TRB consensus sequences of section 2
mg_thymus_bulk_*.tsv.gz Bulk BCR-seq of the thymus, and of blood at the thymectomy and 12 months later (a subset)
mg_thymus_slice*_gc_polygons.csv Hand-drawn outlines of the eGCs in each section
mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz cell2location cell-type proportions for each spot
mg_thymus_slice2_reads.tsv.gz A sample of read-level IgBLAST output for the processing vignette

The receptor files are AIRR rearrangement tables from the SIRUP paper. To keep the package small, the Seurat objects hold a few hundred genes and a reduced H&E image.

This vignette uses section 2 only. The multi-sample vignette uses both sections and the bulk data.

library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))
thymus
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 506 features across 3203 samples within 2 assays 
#> Active assay: Spatial (449 features, 0 variable features)
#>  2 layers present: counts, data
#>  1 other assay present: alra
#>  1 spatial field of view present: thymus_slice2

bcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz"))
bcrs |>
  select(sequence_id, v_call, j_call, c_call, consensus_count, cc_bc_umi) |>
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   sequence_id         v_call             j_call c_call consensus_count cc_bc_umi
#>   <chr>               <chr>              <chr>  <chr>            <int> <chr>    
#> 1 9,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT  IGHV2-5*02         IGHJ4… IGHG1                1 2        
#> 2 11,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT IGHV3-30*03,IGHV3… IGHJ4… IGHG1                1 5        
#> 3 2,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT  IGHV5-51*01        IGHJ5… IGHG2                1 4        
#> 4 6,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT  IGHV5-51*01        IGHJ5… IGHG2                1 2        
#> 5 5,CCTACATTCACAGACG  IGHV3-23*01,IGHV3… IGHJ4… IGHG1                1 6        
#> 6 3,CCTACATTCACAGACG  IGHV1-2*02,IGHV1-… IGHJ4… IGHG1                1 8

Each row is one consensus BCR sequence. cc_bc_umi is the number of reads behind it. The pipeline wrote the spot barcode into sequence_id, after the comma. extractSpatialIds() copies it into its own column, and the suffix argument adds -1 so that it matches the spot names in the Seurat object:

bcrs <- extractSpatialIds(
  bcrs,
  id = "sequence_id",
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
  suffix = "-1"
)

head(colnames(thymus))
#> [1] "AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1" "AAACACCAATAACTGC-1" "AAACAGCTTTCAGAAG-1"
#> [4] "AAACAGGGTCTATATT-1" "AAACAGTGTTCCTGGG-1" "AAACATGGTGAGAGGA-1"
mean(bcrs$barcode_10x %in% colnames(thymus))
#> [1] 0.9373849

A few sequences have a barcode that is not in the Seurat object. The spot was off the tissue or failed the expression QC. SIRUP keeps these rows in the table, but it cannot put them on the tissue.

Keep the high-quality sequences. These are the thresholds from the SIRUP paper (see vignette("processing", package = "SIRUP")):

bcrs <- filterAirr(
  bcrs,
  locus_val = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 250,
  min_j_length = 30,
  min_junction_length = 10,
  productive_only = TRUE,
  min_consensus_count = NULL,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
)
#> filterAirr kept 2195 of 3801 rows (dropped 1606).
bcrs <- filter(bcrs, !grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))

The last line removes the few sequences with an ambiguous base (such as N) in the junction. scoper, which calls the clones below, needs junctions of A, C, G, and T only.

Create a SIRUP object

createSIRUP() joins the spatial data and the receptor table. You tell it which receptor columns hold the spatial ID, the locus, and (when you have them) the clone and a count or weight:

sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = thymus,
  receptors = bcrs,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  locus = "locus",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  metadata = list(tissue = "MG thymus", section = "slice 2")
)

sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 2,105 receptor sequences x 56 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Analyses:        0

A SIRUP object is a list with five parts:

Part Contents Accessor
spatial The Seurat object getSpatial()
receptors The AIRR table, as a tibble getReceptors()
metadata Field names, image settings, and your own notes x$metadata
polygons Tissue regions, one row per polygon getPolygons()
analyses Any results you choose to keep getAnalysis()

SIRUP records the field names once. After that, SIRUP functions find the spatial ID, clone, and locus columns without more arguments. Your column names do not need to match a convention.

createSIRUP() validates the object. It stops with a clear message if, for example, no receptor barcode matches a spot in the Seurat object.

Call clones

A clone is a group of B cells that descend from one ancestor cell. Many SIRUP functions summarize receptors by clone. SIRUP does not call clones itself. updateReceptors() runs a function on the receptor table and puts the result back in the object. Here it runs scoper::hierarchicalClones(), with the threshold from the SIRUP paper:

sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
#> Running defineClonesScoper in bulk mode and only keep heavy chains
sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 2,105 receptor sequences x 57 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0

The receptor table now has a clone_id column, and SIRUP records it as the clone field. If your clone column has another name, such as clone_family_id, give clone = "clone_family_id" to createSIRUP().

Image settings

Two settings control how SIRUP puts spots on the H&E image:

  • image_scale tells SIRUP which scale factor to use. Use "lowres" or "hires" to match the image stored in the Seurat object. Load10X_Spatial() stores the lowres image by default. The example objects store a lowres image.
  • swap_coords swaps the x and y coordinates. Some older Seurat objects store the coordinates in the opposite order to the image. If your spots form the right shape but sit rotated or mirrored over the H&E, set swap_coords = TRUE.

The object stores both settings. Every plot and spatial statistic reads them from the object, so you set them once.

Look inside the object

summary() gives counts for each part:

summary(sirup)
#> SIRUP summary
#>   Spatial IDs:      3,203
#>   Receptor records: 2,105
#>   Receptor IDs:     868
#>   Matched IDs:      797 (91.8%)
#>   Matched records:  1,965
#>   Stored analyses:  0
#> 
#> Per-sample summary
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   sample  n_spatial_ids n_receptor_records n_receptor_ids n_matched_ids
#>   <chr>           <int>              <int>          <int>         <int>
#> 1 spatial          3203               2105            868           797
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: n_matched_records <int>, id_match_rate <dbl>

The accessors return ordinary objects. You can give them to any function from another package:

getSpatial(sirup)
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 506 features across 3203 samples within 2 assays 
#> Active assay: Spatial (449 features, 0 variable features)
#>  2 layers present: counts, data
#>  1 other assay present: alra
#>  1 spatial field of view present: thymus_slice2

getReceptors(sirup) |>
  count(c_call, sort = TRUE) |>
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   c_call     n
#>   <chr>  <int>
#> 1 IGHG1   1172
#> 2 IGHG2    346
#> 3 IGHA1    215
#> 4 IGHM     193
#> 5 IGHG3    117
#> 6 <NA>      19

spatialReceptorSummary() gives a short report of a receptor table:

spatialReceptorSummary(getReceptors(sirup), spatial_id = "barcode_10x")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   n_sequences n_spatial_ids n_loci n_productive
#>         <int>         <int>  <int>        <int>
#> 1        2105           868      1         2105

Plot expression and receptors on the tissue

spatialExpressionPlot() draws gene expression over the H&E image. By default it hides spots with zero expression, so the tissue stays visible.

AICDA marks germinal center B cells. The example objects have two assays: Spatial (counts and log-normalized data) and alra (ALRA-imputed values for a panel of marker genes). Imputed values give smoother maps. Use them for display only, not for statistics.

spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  title = "AICDA"
)

plotReceptors() draws receptor-positive spots. The group argument names the receptor column that sets the color. Here every row has the locus IGH, so all BCR-positive spots get one color:

plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  group = "locus",
  colors = "#0072B2",
  receptor_size = 1.2,
  title = "BCR-positive spots"
)

Use group_val to show only some values of the group column. This plot shows the three largest clones in the section:

top_clones <- getReceptors(sirup) |>
  count(clone_id, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(clone_id)
top_clones
#> [1] "34"  "288" "196"

plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  group = "clone_id",
  group_val = top_clones,
  receptor_size = 1.6,
  title = "Three largest BCR clones"
)

A Visium spot can hold BCRs from more than one clone. When two selected clones share a spot, plotReceptors() gives the spot a combined label, with the clone IDs joined by +. The overlap argument controls this behavior.

plotReceptorsExpression() combines the two plots. Spots with expression are filled points. Receptor-positive spots are hollow rings on top:

plotReceptorsExpression(
  sirup,
  group = "locus",
  gene = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  colors = "#0072B2",
  receptor_size = 1.2,
  title = "AICDA expression and BCR-positive spots"
)

Add tissue regions

Most spatial questions are about regions: a germinal center, a tumor margin, a lesion. In SIRUP a region is a polygon on the tissue image.

Draw polygons

selectSpatialPolygons() opens an app in your web browser. The app shows the spots of the section over the H&E image. A gene or a metadata column sets the spot colors, so you can see the region that you want to outline. We drew the eGCs over imputed AICDA expression, which marks germinal center B cells:

gc_vertices <- selectSpatialPolygons(
  sirup,
  feature = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  plot_image = TRUE,
  save_path = "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"
)

The panel on the left controls the display. Assay, Layer, and Feature choose the values that color the spots. Point size, Point opacity, Show image, and Show zero points change how the spots look. CSV path is the file that the app writes when you finish.

To draw a region, click around its edge. Each click snaps to the nearest spot and adds a vertex (white points below). The app joins the vertices in the order that you click them. Close polygon joins the last vertex to the first:

The other buttons:

  • New polygon closes the current polygon and starts the next one. The app names polygons 1, 2, 3, and so on. To use your own name, type it in Polygon name before you click. Each name must be different.
  • Remove last point removes the last vertex of the current polygon.
  • Reset removes all the polygons.
  • Done closes all open polygons, writes the vertices to the CSV path, and closes the app.

The table under the buttons lists the vertices of the current polygon. When you click Done, selectSpatialPolygons() returns the vertices of every polygon as a data frame: one row per vertex, with the spot (spatial_id), its image coordinates (x, y), and the polygon name (polygon).

Keep the CSV file. It is the record of your annotation, so you and other people can repeat the analysis without drawing again. The regions vignette has more options for the app, for example for large Visium HD sections or a remote server.

Attach polygons to the object

addPolygons() attaches polygons to the object. Give it the data frame from the app (polygons = gc_vertices) or the CSV file (polygons_path). It then annotates every spot and every receptor with the polygon that contains it. The example data include the eGC polygons that we drew for the SIRUP paper:

sirup <- addPolygons(
  sirup,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)

getPolygons(sirup)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   polygon_id vertices        
#>   <chr>      <named list>    
#> 1 1          <tibble [7 × 5]>
#> 2 2          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 3 3          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 4 4          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 5 5          <tibble [6 × 5]>
#> 6 6          <tibble [7 × 5]>
#> 7 7          <tibble [7 × 5]>
#> 8 8          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 9 9          <tibble [4 × 5]>

plotSpatialPolygons(sirup, polygon_alpha = 0.3)

The receptor table now has a polygon_id column. Receptors outside every polygon get NA:

getReceptors(sirup) |>
  count(polygon_id)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   polygon_id     n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 1             28
#> 2 2             23
#> 3 3             14
#> 4 5             47
#> 5 6              4
#> 6 7             30
#> 7 8              6
#> 8 9              4
#> 9 <NA>        1949

A first regional analysis

polygonReceptorSummary() counts the receptors, spots, and clones in each polygon. It stores the result in the object as an analysis:

sirup <- polygonReceptorSummary(sirup, polygon_id = "polygon_id")
getAnalysis(sirup, "polygon_receptor_summary")
#> # A tibble: 9 × 5
#>   polygon_id n_receptors n_spatial_ids n_clones top_clone_fraction
#>   <chr>            <int>         <int>    <int>              <dbl>
#> 1 1                   28             6       16              0.143
#> 2 2                   23             3       16              0.174
#> 3 3                   14             3        8              0.286
#> 4 4                    0             0        0             NA    
#> 5 5                   47            12       23              0.128
#> 6 6                    4             4        4              0.25 
#> 7 7                   30             8       12              0.167
#> 8 8                    6             3        4              0.333
#> 9 9                    4             3        4              0.25

Clonal dominance asks how much of each region the largest clones take up. spatialCloneDominance() computes the fraction of each polygon’s receptors that belongs to each clone. plotSpatialPolygonPies() draws one pie chart per polygon next to the tissue:

dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(object = sirup)

dominance$dominance |>
  group_by(polygon) |>
  slice_max(proportion, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(polygon, clone_id, n_receptors, proportion)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#> # Groups:   polygon [8]
#>   polygon clone_id n_receptors proportion
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 1       928                4      0.143
#> 2 2       381                4      0.174
#> 3 3       196                4      0.286
#> 4 5       810                6      0.128
#> 5 6       136                1      0.25 
#> 6 7       739                5      0.167
#> 7 8       242                2      0.333
#> 8 9       222                1      0.25

pies <- plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  fill = "clone_id",
  top_n = 5
)
pies$page_1
#> Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_text()`).

The function returns one plot per page, with six pies on each page. The top_n argument sets how many clones get their own color in each pie. The other clones go into the grey Other slice.

The eGCs in this section are polyclonal. In the larger eGCs, the largest clone holds 13% to 17% of the BCRs.

Change the data with your own functions

SIRUP does not wrap every AIRR tool. Instead, three functions let you run any function on one part of the object and put the result back:

  • updateReceptors(x, fun, ...) calls fun(getReceptors(x), ...) and stores the returned table.
  • updateSpatial(x, fun, ...) calls fun(getSpatial(x), ...) and stores the returned Seurat object.
  • updateAnalysis(x, name, fun, ...) does the same for a stored analysis.

Each function validates the object again before it returns. For example, updateReceptors() with dplyr::filter() keeps only the class-switched IgG sequences:

igg <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, grepl("^IGHG", c_call))
nrow(getReceptors(igg))
#> [1] 1651

The same pattern runs germline reconstruction (dowser::createGermlines()) or mutation counting (shazam::observedMutations()) inside the object. The clones vignette shows these steps.

updateSpatial() works the same way for the Seurat object. This call adds the cell2location cell-type proportions as spot metadata:

cell_types <- data.table::fread(
  file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz"),
  data.table = FALSE
)
cell_types <- filter(cell_types, sample == "mg_thymus_slice2")
rownames(cell_types) <- cell_types$barcode
cell_types <- select(cell_types, -sample, -barcode)

sirup <- updateSpatial(sirup, Seurat::AddMetaData, metadata = cell_types)

spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "GC B",
  zero_tol = 0.05,
  title = "GC B cell proportion (cell2location)"
)

spatialExpressionPlot() accepts genes and numeric spot metadata columns. zero_tol hides spots at or below a value. Here it hides spots with less than 5% GC B cells.

Keep results with the data

setAnalysis() stores any R object under a name. Stored results stay with the data that produced them, so you do not need to track separate files:

sirup <- setAnalysis(sirup, "gc_dominance", dominance)
listAnalyses(sirup)
#> [1] "polygon_receptor_summary" "gc_dominance"

saveSIRUP() writes the object to one RDS file. readSIRUP() reads it back, validates it, and upgrades objects that an older SIRUP version saved:

path <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_thymus_slice2.sirup.rds")
saveSIRUP(sirup, path)
sirup <- readSIRUP(path)
sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 2,105 receptor sequences x 67 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        2
#> Polygons:        9

Next steps

  • To process your own reads, read vignette("processing", package = "SIRUP").
  • To draw regions and compare their repertoires, read vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP").
  • To test spatial patterns, read vignette("spatial-statistics", package = "SIRUP").
  • To build lineage trees and show them on the tissue, read vignette("clones-and-trees", package = "SIRUP").
  • To combine sections, bulk BCR-seq, and blood, read vignette("multisample", package = "SIRUP").
